cards.definition: One or more notes that come before the first full bar of a piece; also called a pick-up or upbeat.
Stepwise melodic movement where notes move by small intervals (one or two semitones), creating a smooth, flowing melody.
Angular melodic movement where notes leap by larger intervals, creating a more dramatic or jagged effect.
The notes of a chord played one after another rather than simultaneously, creating a rippling effect.
A melody that moves up or down a scale in stepwise motion; can be ascending or descending.
The distance between the highest and lowest notes in a melody; a wide range gives more expressive possibility.
A melodic or harmonic pattern that is repeated at a higher or lower pitch level.
When a melodic idea introduced by one part is echoed or repeated by another part, often at a different pitch.
A short recurring musical theme associated with a character, place or idea, especially in film and opera.
A short, recurring melodic or rhythmic idea that forms the basis of a longer piece of music.
The interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency; 12 semitones apart.
An interval of two semitones; the distance between adjacent notes in most major and minor scales.
An interval of four semitones; creates a bright, happy sound when used harmonically.
An interval of five semitones; has a strong, open sound and is found in many fanfares.
An interval of seven semitones; a very stable, hollow-sounding interval used in power chords and drones.
An interval of nine semitones; often sounds warm and expressive in melodic writing.
An interval of eleven semitones; creates tension that resolves to the octave.
The smallest standard interval in Western music; the distance between adjacent keys on a piano.
Melody that moves in semitone steps using notes outside the main key, creating colour and tension.
A five-note scale (e.g. C D E G A) widely used in folk, blues, rock and non-Western music.
Flattened 3rd, 5th or 7th scale degrees used in blues and jazz to create an expressive, bending sound.
Rapid alternation between a note and the one above it; decoration added to a melody for expressive effect.
A secondary melody played at the same time as the main melody, providing harmonic and rhythmic contrast.
A melodic phrase that responds to an opening phrase, creating a question-and-answer effect.
Music built around a recognisable theme that is developed, varied and revisited throughout a piece.
A short, loud melodic passage using the notes of a major chord, typically performed by brass instruments.
An interval smaller than a semitone; common in non-Western music and some contemporary classical works.
Repeating a melodic or rhythmic idea to create unity and help listeners recognise a theme.
Introducing new or opposing musical ideas (e.g. different pitch, tempo or dynamics) to maintain interest.
The frequency of a sound; high pitch is fast vibration, low pitch is slow vibration — affects mood and register.
A scale or key with a bright, happy sound, built on the pattern T T S T T T S (tones and semitones).
A scale or key with a darker, sadder sound; has a flattened third degree compared to major.
Changing from one key to another during a piece of music.
The fifth degree of the scale; the dominant chord (V) creates tension that resolves to the tonic.
Major and minor keys that share the same key signature; e.g. C major and A minor are relatives.
The three most important chords in a key: tonic (I), subdominant (IV) and dominant (V).
The less common chords built on other degrees of the scale (II, III, VI, VII).
A chord where a note other than the root is in the bass; 1st inversion has the 3rd in the bass.
Music using only the notes of the key; does not use accidentals or notes outside the scale.
The first and most important note/chord of a key; the home note to which music naturally returns.
The fourth degree of the scale and its chord (IV); creates a softer, less tense feeling than the dominant.
A dominant chord with an added flattened 7th, creating strong tension that resolves to the tonic.
A chord progression moving from V to I; sounds final and conclusive, like a full stop in music.
A cadence that ends on chord V; sounds unfinished or questioning, like a comma in music.
A cadence moving from chord IV to I; has a gentle, 'Amen' quality often used in hymns.
A cadence that moves from V to any chord other than I (often VI), creating a surprise effect.
A sequence of chords played in a specific order, forming the harmonic foundation of a piece.
The rate at which chords change in a piece; fast harmonic rhythm creates energy, slow creates stability.
A sustained note, usually in the bass, held while other parts move above it.
A sustained or repeated note (usually the tonic or dominant) in the bass while harmonies change above.
A harsh, clashing sound created by intervals or chords that create tension and want to resolve.
A chord using only the root and perfect 5th (no 3rd), common in rock music; neither major nor minor.
A five-note scale with no semitones; used widely in folk, blues, rock and non-Western music for its open sound.
A two-section structure (A B) where each section is usually repeated; common in Baroque dance movements.
A three-section structure (A B A) where the opening section returns after a contrasting middle section.
A structure where a main theme (A) keeps returning between contrasting episodes: A B A C A D A.
A three-section form (Minuet – Trio – Minuet) in triple time, common in Classical symphonies and sonatas.
A form where an opening theme is followed by a series of varied versions of that theme.
A song structure where the same music is used for each verse of the text.
A popular song structure with four 8-bar sections: verse, verse, bridge, verse — common in jazz standards.
A chord progression lasting 12 bars using chords I, IV and V; the foundation of blues and early rock and roll.
A musical conversation where a phrase (call) is answered by another phrase (response); common in blues and gospel.
A short melodic, harmonic or rhythmic pattern that is persistently repeated throughout a piece.
A contrasting section in a song that links verses or provides harmonic/melodic variety before the final chorus.
A short solo or instrumental passage in popular music where the main accompaniment drops out.
A repeated section of audio or MIDI that forms the rhythmic or harmonic basis of electronic and dance music.
Creating and performing music spontaneously without written notation, central to jazz and blues.
A repeated section of a song with the same music but different lyrics each time, advancing the narrative.
A repeated section of a song with the same music and lyrics, usually the most memorable part.
An eight-bar contrasting section in a pop song that provides variety before the final chorus.
A short rhythmic or melodic flourish (often by drums or guitar) that bridges sections or fills gaps.
An opening passage before the main theme or verse begins, setting the mood and key of the piece.
A concluding section that brings a piece to an end; a coda is a formal ending often extending beyond the main structure.
A short, repeated melodic or rhythmic pattern in rock or jazz that forms the backbone of a piece.
How musical sentences are shaped and grouped; regular phrasing uses equal-length phrases, irregular phrasing varies their length.
A single melodic line with no accompaniment; the simplest texture.
A main melody supported by chords or a harmonic accompaniment moving in a similar rhythm.
Two or more independent melodic lines sounding simultaneously, each of equal importance.
All parts playing or singing the same notes at the same pitch (or in octaves).
A texture where all parts move together rhythmically, like a chorale or hymn.
Building up texture by adding parts one at a time, common in minimalism and electronic music.
A homophonic texture with a clear tune on top and a harmonic or rhythmic accompaniment below.
A high decorative melody sung or played above the main tune.
A simple canon where voices enter at regular intervals singing the same melody, e.g. 'Frère Jacques'.
A form of imitation where a melody is introduced by one part and then imitated by others after a set delay.
A broken chord accompaniment pattern (low-high-middle-high) commonly used in Classical-era keyboard music.
Short, sharp chords played on an off-beat, common in jazz, funk and pop music.
A bass line that moves in steady crotchets with a smooth, stepwise or arpeggiated pattern; typical in jazz.
A Baroque accompaniment technique using a bass instrument and a keyboard to improvise harmonies from a figured bass.
Fast tempo markings; Allegro means lively and quick, Vivace means very lively and brisk.
A moderately fast tempo, slightly slower than Allegro.
Moderate tempo markings; Moderato means at a moderate pace, Andante means walking pace.
Slow tempo markings; Adagio means slow and stately, Lento means very slow.
A gradual increase in tempo, getting faster.
A gradual decrease in tempo, getting slower; both terms are interchangeable in most contexts.
Flexibility in tempo where notes are pushed and pulled for expressive effect, common in Romantic music.
A symbol indicating the performer should hold a note or rest for longer than its written value.
A note worth four beats in 4/4 time; the longest standard note value.
A note worth two beats in 4/4 time; half the value of a semibreve.
A note worth one beat in 4/4 time; the most common beat unit.
A note worth half a beat in 4/4 time; two quavers equal one crotchet.
A note worth a quarter of a beat in 4/4 time; four semiquavers equal one crotchet.
A note followed by a dot, which adds half its value again (e.g. a dotted crotchet = 1.5 beats).
Placing rhythmic stress on normally weak beats or between beats, creating a surprise or off-beat feel.
A performance style where paired quavers are played unevenly (long-short), common in jazz.
Three notes played in the time of two of the same value, creating a flowing or galloping feel.
A rhythmic pattern from Bhangra music; a driving 8-beat cycle played on the dhol drum.
Energetic, relentless rhythmic patterns that propel music forward, common in rock and dance music.
Rhythmic patterns associated with specific dances, e.g. waltz (3/4), tango, samba.
A consistent, predictable pattern of strong and weak beats organised into equal-length bars.
Time signatures that do not divide equally into groups of two or three, e.g. 5/4 or 7/8.
Time signatures where the beat divides into two equal parts, e.g. 2/4, 3/4, 4/4.
Time signatures where the beat divides into three equal parts, e.g. 6/8, 9/8, 12/8.
Metre with two beats per bar, e.g. 2/4.
Metre with three beats per bar, e.g. 3/4; gives a waltz-like feeling.
Metre with four beats per bar, e.g. 4/4; the most common time signature in Western music.
Extra emphasis placed on a note or beat, making it stand out; shown by the symbol >.
Very quiet; one of the softest dynamic markings.
Quiet; a soft dynamic level.
Moderately quiet; louder than piano but quieter than mezzo forte.
Moderately loud; the most common dynamic level in everyday performance.
Loud; a strong, full dynamic level.
Very loud; one of the loudest standard dynamic markings.
A gradual increase in volume, getting louder.
A gradual decrease in volume, getting quieter; also called decrescendo.
A sudden, strong accent on a single note or chord, giving it extra force.
The broad tradition of composed music in Europe from the Medieval period to the present day.
A period of Western classical music (c.1600–1750) characterised by ornamentation, basso continuo and counterpoint, e.g. Bach, Handel.
A period of Western classical music (c.1750–1820) characterised by balance, clarity and formal structures, e.g. Mozart, Haydn.
A period of Western classical music (c.1820–1900) characterised by emotional expression, large orchestras and programme music, e.g. Beethoven, Brahms.
Classical music written for a small ensemble to be performed in an intimate setting, e.g. a string quartet.
A genre originating in early 20th-century America, characterised by improvisation, swing rhythms and complex harmonies.
An African-American music genre using the 12-bar blues, blue notes and call and response; influenced rock and jazz.
A theatrical genre combining songs, spoken dialogue, acting and dance to tell a story on stage.
Music composed specifically to accompany and enhance a film, using leitmotifs and orchestral scoring.
A genre developed from rock and roll in the 1960s, typically using electric guitars, bass and drums with a strong backbeat.
A genre combining gospel and R&B, characterised by passionate vocals, call and response and strong rhythmic feel.
A genre originating in 1970s New York, featuring rap vocals, turntablism, sampling and electronic beats.
A Jamaican genre characterised by off-beat rhythms (skank), heavy bass and lyrics often addressing social issues.
A slow, emotional song that tells a story; common in pop, rock and classical traditions.
Popular music aimed at a mainstream audience, characterised by verse-chorus structure, catchy melodies and simple harmonies.
A vibrant Punjabi music and dance genre, featuring the dhol drum, rapid tempo and energetic performance.
Music that combines elements from two or more different genres or cultural traditions.
A 20th-century style using simple repeated patterns (ostinati) with gradual change over long periods, e.g. Philip Glass.
A single performer playing or singing alone, or taking a prominent melodic role.
A piece performed by two musicians.
The highest female or treble voice type.
The lower female voice type; also used to describe instruments in a middle register.
The higher male voice type.
The lowest male voice type; also refers to the lowest instrument in a group.
Voices that support the lead vocalist, often singing harmonies or repeated phrases.
Singing without instrumental accompaniment.
A large ensemble of instruments grouped into strings, woodwind, brass and percussion sections.
A chamber ensemble of two violins, viola and cello; a standard classical grouping.
A small ensemble typically including electric guitar, bass guitar, drums and vocals.
Sounds produced or modified electronically, using synthesisers, samplers or digital audio workstations.
Placing sounds to the left or right of the stereo field in a recording.
An electronic effect where two identical sounds are gradually moved out of sync, creating a sweeping effect.
A recording of a sound or piece of music used in a new composition; central to hip-hop and electronic music.
An effect that simulates the sound of a space by adding reflected echoes to a sound.
A distinct repetition of a sound after a delay; can be natural or added electronically.
Sound that has been electronically increased in volume using microphones or pickups.
A vocal style where each syllable of text is set to one note.
A vocal style where a single syllable is sung over many notes, creating an ornamental, flowing effect.
A jazz vocal technique using improvised nonsense syllables instead of words.
A rapid, slight variation in pitch used by singers and instrumentalists to add warmth and expression.
A male singing technique that extends the voice above its normal range into a lighter, head-voice register.
A powerful, chest-driven singing technique used in musical theatre to project strongly.
A rhythmic, spoken or chanted vocal style used in hip-hop, often with rhyme and wordplay over a beat.
Playing notes in a short, detached manner, indicated by a dot above or below the note.
Playing notes in a smooth, connected manner with no gaps between them.
Plucking the strings of a bowed instrument instead of using the bow.
Playing a stringed instrument with the bow, as opposed to pizzicato.
An instruction for a string section to split into two or more parts, each playing different notes.
Playing two strings simultaneously on a bowed instrument, creating a fuller, harmonic sound.
Rapid repetition of a single note (strings: rapid bowing; other instruments: rapid restriking).
An electronic effect that clips or overdrives a signal, creating a gritty or fuzzy guitar sound common in rock.
A guitar technique where a note is produced by tapping a finger onto the fretboard without picking.
Striking the rim and head of a drum simultaneously, producing a sharp cracking sound.
A bass guitar technique where the thumb slaps the string against the fretboard for a percussive attack.
Dampening the strings or instrument to reduce sustain and create a softer, more muffled tone.
Sliding continuously between two pitches, either on a stringed instrument or voice.
Smoothly changing the pitch of a note above or below its standard value, common in blues guitar and electronic music.
Singing with the mouth closed, producing a warm, resonant tone.
Holding a note for its full duration or beyond, creating a continuous, smooth sound.
Rapid alternating strokes on a drum creating a continuous, sustained sound.
